title: Wearer may be unaware they are continuously sharing sensitive telemetry
description: By wearing the device, the user continuously provides heart rate, step count, GPS location, and timestamps to the wearable. The sharing may occur passively and continuously, so the wearer may not fully realize the extent, frequency, sensitivity, or persistence of the data disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the device begins or continues collection during normal wear without sufficiently salient, granular, or ongoing notice about what telemetry is captured and when.

title: Wearer may lack meaningful consent or control over continuous telemetry sharing
description: Continuous capture of physiological and location telemetry can exceed what the wearer expects when merely wearing the device. If collection starts by default or bundles multiple sensor types together, the user may be unable to give specific, informed, and freely given consent for each category of data shared to the device.
assumptions: Assumes consent is implicit in wearing/activating the device, or controls are not granular enough to separately enable or disable heart-rate, step, GPS, and timestamp collection.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; exact Nc subtree id may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Telemetry on this flow can link multiple observations to the same wearer
description: The combination of heart-rate patterns, step counts, GPS position, and timestamps in a continuous stream can act as a persistent behavioral signature. Even without an explicit name in the payload, repeated observations on this flow can be linked together as belonging to the same individual or device.
assumptions: Assumes the telemetry stream contains stable identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or sufficiently distinctive spatiotemporal patterns.
uncertainty_note: Exact L subtree id is chosen by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the relevant threat-tree excerpt.

uncertainty_note: Exact I subtree id is chosen by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the relevant threat-tree excerpt.

These inferences may go beyond what the wearer intended to disclose by merely wearing the device.

description: Continuous collection of heart rate, steps, GPS, and timestamps may be excessive relative to a specific feature in use. If the device receives and retains all sensor streams by default, the wearer may be exposed to unnecessary disclosure of personal data beyond what is needed for the current purpose.

title: Excessive disclosure of detailed activity and location data to the companion app
description: The wearable device shares exercise sessions, GPS traces, device identifier, and timestamps with the companion app. If the app does not strictly need raw GPS traces, persistent device identifiers, or full timestamp granularity for its stated purpose, the device's act of sending the full batch violates data minimization and causes avoidable disclosure of sensitive personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the companion app could fulfill core sync or user-feedback functions with less detailed, less granular, or pseudonymized data.

title: Identification via persistent device identifier and unique movement patterns in transit
description: The flow contains a device id plus GPS traces and timestamps. Even if the payload omits a direct real-world name, these attributes can identify the user because persistent identifiers and distinctive mobility patterns can single out an individual.
assumptions: Assumes the device id is stable across syncs and that GPS/time-series data are sufficiently granular to enable singling out.

title: Linkability of multiple exercise sessions and locations across sync events
description: Stable device identifiers, repeated timestamps, and recurring GPS traces allow records from different sync batches to be linked to the same person or device over time. This enables construction of longitudinal behavior profiles across sessions.

description: Even aside from payload contents, the existence, timing, size, and frequency of sync traffic can reveal when the user exercised, traveled, or was active. An observer of the communication channel may detect sensitive behavioral events from these metadata.
